title: Transpiration
tagline: How and where a plant loses water, what controls the loss, and how you measure it with a potometer.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Every factor, adaptation and apparatus below is standard plant physiology. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, and although it sounds like a waste it is the engine that pulls water and dissolved minerals from the soil to the top of the plant. This chapter separates the three routes of loss — stomatal, cuticular and lenticular — and explains the mechanism of the stomatal pore, including why guard cells open and close as they do. It then examines the environmental factors that govern the rate, describes Ganong's potometer as the standard apparatus and states honestly what it actually measures, and finishes with the significance of transpiration and the adaptations xerophytes use to prevent the plant from losing too much.

learningOutcomes: Define transpiration and distinguish its stomatal, cuticular and lenticular types.
Explain how guard cells open and close the stomatal pore.
Investigate the effect of light, temperature, humidity, wind and leaf area on the rate of transpiration.
Describe Ganong's potometer, state what it measures, and outline the significance of transpiration and the adaptations that limit it.

learn.title: Types of transpiration and the mechanism of the stomatal pore

blocks.text: Transpiration is defined as the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, and it is distinguished from guttation, which is the loss of liquid water. There are three routes. Stomatal transpiration passes through the stomatal pores and accounts for the overwhelming majority of the total, because the pores are numerous and their aperture is under the plant's control. Cuticular transpiration occurs directly through the waxy cuticle that covers the epidermis, and in a plant with a thick cuticle this route is very small. Lenticular transpiration takes place through the lenticels, the porous openings in the bark of woody stems, and is the least significant of the three. The stomatal pore itself is flanked by two guard cells, which in most dicots are kidney shaped and differ from ordinary epidermal cells in containing chloroplasts and having unevenly thickened walls — the wall on the side away from the pore is thicker and less elastic. When the guard cells take in water and become turgid, the thinner outer wall bulges outwards and pulls the thicker inner wall with it, opening the pore; when they lose water and become flaccid, the walls recoil and the pore closes.

items.meaning: Loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.
A pore in the epidermis flanked by two guard cells, controlling gas exchange and water loss.
One of the two kidney- or dumbbell-shaped cells surrounding a stoma; the only epidermal cell with chloroplasts in most dicots.

items: The guard cells of most dicots are kidney shaped; in grasses they are dumbbell shaped and flanked by subsidiary cells.
Guard cells contain chloroplasts and can photosynthesise, which distinguishes them from all other epidermal cells.
Their outer wall is thin and the inner wall facing the pore is thick, so differential bulging opens the pore.
In light the guard cells photosynthesise, sugars accumulate, water enters by osmosis and the pore opens.
At night sugars are converted to starch, osmotic pressure falls, water leaves and the pore closes.
Carbon dioxide concentration also plays a part: a fall in carbon dioxide in the leaf promotes opening.
Stomata open in the day for photosynthesis, and water loss is the unavoidable cost of taking in carbon dioxide.
Most stomata are on the lower epidermis, which reduces water loss because that surface is shaded and cooler.

items.text: A plant kept in darkness through the day has closed stomata and loses far less water, which is why cut flowers last longer in the shade and why wilting is slower indoors than in hot sun.
items.note: Darkness closes the stomata because no sugars are being made to hold water in the guard cells.

items.text: A leaf of a grass species shows guard cells shaped like dumbbells with a subsidiary cell at each end, so the pore is opened by the swelling of the thickened ends rather than by a simple arching.
items.note: Two guard-cell shapes are worth learning because grasses are the standard monocot example.

learn.title: Factors that affect the rate of transpiration

blocks.text: The rate of transpiration depends on a set of external factors that act on the evaporation of water from the leaf, and one internal factor that sets the ceiling. Light is the most important external factor, because it opens the stomata: in bright light the pores are wide and the rate rises, while in darkness they close and the rate falls to the small cuticular loss. Temperature increases the rate because it raises the kinetic energy of the water molecules, so they evaporate and diffuse faster, and warm air also holds more vapour so the gradient out of the leaf steepens. Humidity acts in the opposite direction: the drier the air outside the leaf, the steeper the gradient of water vapour from the saturated intercellular spaces to the atmosphere, and the faster the loss. Wind removes the saturated layer of air that clings to the leaf surface, replacing it with drier air, so a breeze increases transpiration until the wind becomes strong enough to force the stomata shut mechanically. The internal factor is leaf area, since a plant with more leaf surface has more stomata available. Soil water supply and the root system set what the plant can replace.

items: The three factors that raise the rate in a typical day are light, high temperature and low humidity.
A hot, dry, windy day produces the fastest transpiration and is when a plant is most likely to wilt.
Wilting occurs when water loss exceeds absorption, so the mesophyll cells lose turgor faster than the roots can supply water.
An internal factor such as leaf area determines the potential rate while external factors determine the actual rate at a given moment.
A plant with a thick cuticle has low cuticular loss, so its total transpiration is dominated by the stomatal route.
Opening stomata to take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis inevitably exposes the wet inner surface of the leaf to dry air.
Root density and soil moisture set the supply side, which is why drought closes stomata before the plant dries out.
In an experiment, all factors but the one under test must be held constant, or the result cannot be attributed to that factor.

items.text: A potted plant in a bright warm room wilts by midday while an identical plant beside it in the shade stays firm, because light and temperature both raised the rate above what the roots could replace.
items.note: Two factors changed together, which is exactly why a controlled experiment holds them.

items.text: Placing a cut stem in water and enclosing the leaves in a clear bag collects droplets on the bag within an hour, demonstrating that the vapour comes from the leaves rather than from the soil surface.
items.note: Bagging the pot surface as a control rules out evaporation from the soil.

blocks.text: Ganong's potometer is the standard school apparatus for measuring the rate of transpiration. It consists of a funnel-shaped reservoir fitted with a rubber stopper through which the cut shoot passes, a horizontal graduated capillary tube connected to the reservoir, and a small outlet at one end to remove any air bubble. Water fills the apparatus completely, the shoot is cut under water so that no air is drawn into the xylem, and the cut end is pushed through the stopper so that no water can escape past it except by passing into the plant. As the shoot transpires, water is drawn up from the reservoir and a meniscus moves along the graduated tube. The rate is calculated by measuring the distance the meniscus travels in a given time and converting it to volume using the calibration of the tube, giving millilitres of water absorbed per unit time. Critically, the potometer measures the rate of water uptake by the shoot, not transpiration directly: the two are close but not identical, because a small proportion of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis, in the building of new tissue, and in maintaining the cells' own turgor.

items: The shoot must be cut under water, otherwise an air embolism enters the xylem and breaks the continuous water column.
The potometer records water uptake, which is only an approximation of transpiration because some water is retained and used.
A capillary tube is used because even a tiny uptake then produces a large, easily readable movement of the meniscus.
To compare treatments, the same shoot or identical shoots must be used with all other conditions held constant.
An air bubble in the tube must be removed before starting, since it would compress and distort the readings.
Measuring over a fixed time interval and repeating gives a rate rather than a single distance.
Water loss through the cut surface must be prevented by a tight seal, or the reading overestimates transpiration.
The apparatus is sealed, so water can leave only through the leaves of the shoot.

items.text: Placing the whole potometer in a sealed polythene bag with a wet towel gives a humid still-air condition, and comparing its meniscus movement with an identical apparatus in bright warm air shows the effect of humidity alone.
items.note: The same shoot type and a fixed time interval are what make the two readings comparable.

items.text: Moving a potometer into a fan's airflow speeds the meniscus markedly, showing that removal of the saturated air layer increases the gradient out of the leaf.
items.note: Wind acts on the outside of the leaf, not on the guard cells.

learn.title: Why transpiration matters and how plants limit it

blocks.text: Transpiration matters for four reasons. It provides the transpiration pull, the main force lifting water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the top of the plant, because evaporation at the leaf surface creates a tension that is transmitted down the continuous xylem column. It cools the plant, since the latent heat of vaporisation is taken from the leaf, which matters greatly in hot, sunny conditions. It maintains the turgor of the cells and so keeps soft tissues expanded, and it aids the distribution of minerals, which arrive dissolved in the transpiration stream. Yet the same process can kill a plant, so xerophytes — plants adapted to dry habitats — carry a suite of structures that reduce loss while still allowing gas exchange. These include a thick waxy cuticle, a reduced leaf surface often modified into spines as in cactus, sunken stomata lying in pits where a pocket of humid air is trapped, hairs on the leaf surface that hold a still moist layer over the pores, and rolled leaves that enclose the stomata in a sheltered channel. Each adaptation reduces the gradient between the inside of the leaf and the air without abolishing carbon dioxide entry.

blocks.caption: Adaptations that reduce transpiration and how each works
rows: Covers the epidermis with an impermeable layer, cutting cuticular loss
Removes most of the transpiring surface; spines also deter grazing
Pits trap a pocket of humid air, so the vapour gradient out of the pore is small
Hold a still, moist layer of air over the stomata, reducing the gradient
Enclose the stomata within a sheltered channel of humid air
Store dilute sap so water can be used during a dry period
Fewer stomata are exposed to the dry atmosphere
Maintains the water supply so the stomata need not close prematurely

items: Transpiration is often called a necessary evil because the water loss is the unavoidable cost of opening stomata for carbon dioxide.
Well over ninety per cent of the water absorbed by a plant is lost again by transpiration rather than used in photosynthesis.
Only a very small fraction of absorbed water is used in photosynthesis and in building new tissue.
Wilting is temporary if the evening brings lower temperatures and higher humidity, allowing turgor to recover.
Permanent wilting occurs when the soil can no longer supply water at all and the cells are damaged.
The transpiration stream also carries dissolved mineral salts to the leaves, so it serves transport as well as lift.
Cooling by evaporation is especially important for a plant in full sun, where absorbed heat would otherwise damage enzymes.
Every xerophyte adaptation works by lowering the water vapour gradient rather than by sealing the leaf completely.

items.text: A cactus has no broad leaves at all: photosynthesis is carried out by the green stem, the surface is covered by a thick cuticle, and the stomata are sunk into pits — three separate adaptations visible in one plant.
items.note: Name the adaptation and then the mechanism, not just the plant.

items.text: On a hot afternoon a plant in direct sun has leaves cooler than the surrounding air because evaporation takes latent heat away from the leaf surface, which is the same principle that cools a sweating body.
items.note: The physics is identical in both cases; only the route of water loss differs.

keyPoints: Transpiration is the loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.
The three types are stomatal, the greatest, cuticular through the waxy cuticle, and lenticular through lenticels.
Guard cells are the only epidermal cells with chloroplasts in most dicots, and their walls are unevenly thickened.
Guard cells become turgid and the pore opens; they become flaccid and the pore closes.
Light opens the stomata, temperature and wind increase the rate, and high humidity decreases it.
Wilting occurs when water loss exceeds absorption so the mesophyll cells lose turgor.
Ganong's potometer measures water uptake by the shoot, which only approximates the rate of transpiration.
The shoot must be cut under water to prevent an air embolism entering the xylem.
Transpiration provides the pull that lifts water and minerals, and it cools the plant by latent heat of vaporisation.
Xerophytes reduce loss with a thick cuticle, spines, sunken stomata, leaf hairs and rolled leaves, each of which lowers the vapour gradient.
examFocus: The potometer question reliably asks what it measures — water uptake, not transpiration — and the reason the two differ must be given.
Guard cell answers must mention the unequal wall thickening; saying only that they swell loses the mechanism mark.
Factor questions need a reason stated in terms of the vapour gradient or of stomatal aperture, not merely a direction of change.
When asked about adaptations, name the adaptation, the plant that shows it, and the mechanism by which it reduces loss — three parts, three marks.
Do not confuse transpiration with guttation: one is vapour through stomata by day, the other liquid at the leaf margin by night.

vocabulary.meaning: Loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant.
Water loss through the stomatal pores, the largest fraction of the total.
Specialised cell flanking a stoma whose turgor controls the aperture of the pore.
Waxy waterproof layer over the epidermis limiting cuticular loss.
Apparatus that estimates transpiration by measuring water uptake.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the correct description of transpiration?
options: Loss of liquid water from the root surface by evaporation
Loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant
Loss of water through the stomata only, with no other route
Absorption of water by the root hair followed by its transport
questions.answer: Loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant
questions.explanation: Transpiration is specifically the loss of water in vapour form from any aerial part — leaves, stems or flowers — and it occurs by stomatal, cuticular and lenticular routes, not by the stomata alone. Liquid loss through the hydathodes is guttation, while the final option describes absorption and conduction rather than loss.
questions.commonMistake: Restricting transpiration to the stomata. Stomatal loss is the largest part, but cuticular and lenticular loss also occur.

questions.prompt: The stomatal pore opens when the two __________ cells become turgid and closes when they become __________.
questions.explanation: The guard cells control the aperture. When they take in water by osmosis and swell, their thin outer walls bulge outwards and pull the thickened inner walls apart, opening the pore. When they lose water and become flaccid, the walls relax back together and the pore shuts, cutting off both water loss and carbon dioxide entry.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 'epidermal' for the first blank. The pore is bounded only by the two guard cells; ordinary epidermal cells surround but do not form it.

questions.prompt: A plant is moved from still air to a gentle breeze, everything else being equal. What happens to its rate of transpiration and why?
options: It falls, because the wind closes the stomata
It rises, because the saturated layer of air next to the leaf is replaced by drier air
It is unchanged, because the guard cells control the rate
It rises, because wind directly opens the guard cells
questions.answer: It rises, because the saturated layer of air next to the leaf is replaced by drier air
questions.explanation: Still air next to a leaf quickly becomes saturated with water vapour, which flattens the gradient between the wet interior of the leaf and the atmosphere outside. A breeze sweeps that saturated layer away and replaces it with drier air, steepening the gradient so vapour diffuses out faster. Wind does not act on the guard cells directly, and a strong wind can eventually force the stomata shut.
questions.commonMistake: Saying wind opens the stomata. It has no direct effect on them; it acts on the air outside the leaf.

questions.prompt: Explain why a potometer measures the rate of water uptake rather than the rate of transpiration, and state how closely the two agree.
questions.answer: The potometer is a sealed, water-filled apparatus, so any movement of the meniscus along the capillary tube represents water leaving the reservoir and entering the cut shoot. Since the plant takes up water only to replace what it loses and to maintain its tissues, the uptake closely follows the loss. However, not all the water absorbed is transpired: a small proportion is used as a raw material in photosynthesis, a small amount is retained in building new cells, and some remains in the cells to keep them turgid. Water uptake is therefore slightly greater than transpiration, and the potometer gives an approximation of the rate rather than a direct measurement of it.
questions.explanation: Both parts are required: what the apparatus physically records, and the specific reasons uptake exceeds transpiration. Quoting photosynthesis alone earns partial credit, since retention for growth and turgor account for the remainder of the difference.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming the potometer measures transpiration directly. Its central limitation is that it measures uptake, and that is precisely what the question tests.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would use Ganong's potometer to compare the rate of transpiration of a plant in bright light with the rate in darkness, naming the variables you would control.
questions.answer: Cut a leafy shoot under water so that no air enters the xylem, and insert it through the rubber stopper of a potometer filled completely with water, making sure no air bubbles remain in the capillary tube. Record the position of the meniscus, leave the apparatus in bright light for a fixed period, say fifteen minutes, and record the position again; the distance moved, converted to volume using the tube's calibration, gives the uptake in that interval. Repeat to obtain a reliable mean. Then place an identical potometer with an identical shoot in darkness for the same period and measure the movement in the same way. The variables held constant must include the temperature, the humidity and the air movement, since all three affect the rate, together with the leaf area of the shoot and the volume and source of the water. The independent variable is light, and the dependent variable is the distance moved by the meniscus in a fixed time. A smaller movement in darkness indicates a lower rate, because the stomata close when no photosynthesis is taking place.
questions.explanation: The answer must give the cutting-under-water step, the measurement procedure with a fixed time, and the controlled variables, since an uncontrolled temperature or humidity difference would invalidate the comparison. Naming the independent and dependent variables shows an understanding of experimental design rather than only of the apparatus.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting to state which variables are controlled. Two readings taken at different temperatures prove nothing about light.

questions.prompt: Which structure allows most of the water absorbed by a plant to leave it?
options: The waxy cuticle on the leaf
questions.explanation: Stomatal transpiration accounts for the great majority of water loss, because there are very many stomata and their aperture is adjustable. Cuticular loss through the waxy cuticle is small in a plant with a thick cuticle, lenticular loss through bark is smaller still, and root hairs absorb water rather than releasing it.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the cuticle because it covers the largest area. It is waxy and nearly waterproof, so its contribution is minor.

questions.prompt: A desert plant is found to have leaves reduced to spines, a thick waxy cuticle over its green stem, stomata sunk into deep pits, and a dense covering of hairs over those pits. Explain how each of these four features reduces water loss, and state why the plant cannot simply keep its stomata permanently closed.
questions.answer: Reducing the leaves to spines removes almost all of the broad transpiring surface; the spines also deter animals, but their water-saving effect comes from the drastic reduction in the area exposed to dry air. The thick waxy cuticle covering the stem makes the epidermis virtually impermeable, so cuticular transpiration is cut to a minimum across the whole photosynthetic surface. Stomata sunk into deep pits allow gas exchange while trapping a pocket of humid air around each pore, so the vapour gradient between the inside of the leaf and the air immediately outside the stoma is small and diffusion outwards is slow. The hairs over the pits hold a still layer of moist air and reduce air movement across the pore, maintaining that humid pocket even in a breeze, which further flattens the gradient. The plant cannot close its stomata permanently because photosynthesis requires carbon dioxide to enter, and without a supply of carbon dioxide no food can be made and the plant would starve; closing the pores also removes the transpiration stream that cools the plant and carries minerals to the leaves.
questions.explanation: Each of the four features needs its own mechanism, and the mechanisms differ — surface reduction, an impermeable layer, a trapped humid pocket, and still air over that pocket — so treating them as one general point loses credit. The second half demands a reasoned argument about carbon dioxide entry, which is why transpiration is described as a necessary evil.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the hairs stop water loss by absorbing it. They do not absorb the vapour; they trap moist air so that the gradient driving diffusion stays small.

questions.prompt: Give two functions of transpiration for the plant.
questions.answer: Transpiration generates the transpiration pull: evaporation from the leaf surfaces creates a tension that is transmitted down the continuous water column in the xylem, and this is the main force lifting water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the top of the plant. It also cools the plant, because the latent heat required to vaporise the water is taken from the leaf, which protects the enzymes from damage in hot, sunny conditions.
questions.explanation: Both functions must be stated with the reason they work: the pull depends on the continuous column of water in the xylem, and the cooling depends on the heat taken in when water changes state. Giving only that transpiration 'helps transport water' without naming the pull earns partial credit.
questions.commonMistake: Saying transpiration helps plants absorb water from the soil. Absorption at the root is by osmosis; transpiration provides the pull that draws the column upwards.

questions.prompt: When water loss by transpiration exceeds absorption by the roots, the mesophyll cells lose __________ and the plant is said to __________.
questions.explanation: The mesophyll cells depend on a continuous supply of water to keep their vacuoles full and their protoplasts pressed against the walls. When transpiration removes water faster than the roots replace it, the vacuoles shrink, turgor pressure falls and the leaves droop, which is wilting. If water becomes available again and conditions allow, the cells regain turgor and the plant recovers.
questions.commonMistake: Describing wilting as the cells dying. Temporary wilting is reversible as soon as absorption again exceeds loss; only permanent wilting damages the cells.

questions.prompt: A leaf shows stomata situated at the bottom of deep pits with hairs over them, a very thick cuticle, and almost no leaf lamina. What kind of habitat is the plant adapted to, and why?
options: A waterlogged marsh, because the pits keep water out of the leaf
A hot dry habitat, because each feature reduces the water vapour gradient out of the leaf
A deep forest floor, because the hairs trap carbon dioxide
A cold alpine slope, because the cuticle prevents freezing
questions.answer: A hot dry habitat, because each feature reduces the water vapour gradient out of the leaf
questions.explanation: Every feature listed is a xerophytic adaptation: sunken stomata with hairs hold a humid pocket of air so the gradient from the saturated leaf interior to the outside is small, the thick cuticle makes the surface nearly impermeable, and reduced lamina lowers the total area available for loss. Together they let the plant keep its stomata open for carbon dioxide while losing as little water as possible in a dry atmosphere.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the pits to keeping water out. Their function is to hold humid air in, so that the outward vapour gradient is reduced.

questions.prompt: Explain the relationship between transpiration and the ascent of sap in a tall tree, describing the properties of water that make the mechanism possible.
questions.answer: As water evaporates from the wet mesophyll surfaces and escapes through the stomata, the water potential in those cells falls, so water moves in by osmosis from adjacent cells and ultimately from the xylem vessels. This withdrawal places the whole column of water in the xylem under tension, and the tension is transmitted unbroken from the leaves down to the roots, producing the transpiration pull that draws water and dissolved minerals upward. Two properties of water make this possible. Cohesion is the attraction between water molecules, which holds the column together so that it moves as a continuous thread rather than breaking under tension. Adhesion is the attraction of water molecules to the cellulose of the xylem wall, which helps support the column against gravity. Because the column is continuous and cohesive, evaporation at the top can lift water many metres; the same mechanism cannot work in a gas or in a liquid whose molecules do not cohere.
questions.explanation: The chain must run evaporation to falling water potential to tension in the column to upward pull, and the two properties, cohesion and adhesion, must both be named with the role each plays. Quoting transpiration pull without explaining how the tension is transmitted earns only part of the credit.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the xylem as a straw being sucked from above. The mechanism is tension transmitted through a cohesive column, not pressure pushing from the roots.
